plain_english: Someone says, "I hate being pitied." So ask yourself: is being pitied something that concerns you or the people doing the pitying? Well, can you stop them from pitying you? Yes, you can — if you show them you don't need pity. But here's the real question: do you actually deserve pity or not? You probably think you don't. But these people aren't pitying you for the right reasons anyway. They're not pitying you for your character flaws — which would make sense. Instead, they pity you for being poor, for not having important jobs, for being sick, for losing people you love, and things like that. So what will you do? Will you try to convince everyone that none of these things are actually bad — that you can be poor, powerless, and ignored and still be happy? Or will you just try to look rich and powerful to them?
original_excerpt: I am grieved, a man says, at being pitied. Whether then is the fact of your being pitied a thing which concerns you or those who pity you? Well, is it in your power to stop this pity? It is in my power, if I show them that I do not require pity. And whether then are you in the condition of not deserving (requiring) pity, or are you not in that condition? I think that I am not; but these persons do not pity me, for the things for which, if they ought to pity me, it would be proper, I mean, for my faults; but they pity me for my poverty, for not possessing honorable offices, for diseases and deaths and other such things. Whether then are you prepared to convince the many, that not one of these things is an evil, but that it is possible for a man who is poor and has no office ([Greek: anarchonti)] and enjoys no honor to be happy; or to show yourself to them as rich and in power?
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied, Section 1

plain_english: The second path belongs to someone who is boastful, foolish, and worthless. Think about what it takes to keep up this act. You'll need to hire slaves and buy some silver dishes. You'll show them off in public — often the same ones over and over — and try to hide that fact. You'll need fancy clothes and other things just for show. You'll try to look like important people respect you. You'll either eat at their houses or pretend you do. You'll use cheap tricks to make yourself look better and more noble than you really are. This is what you'll have to do if you choose the second path to avoid being pitied.
original_excerpt: For the second of these things belong to a man who is boastful, silly, and good for nothing. And consider by what means the pretence must be supported. It will be necessary for you to hire slaves and to possess a few silver vessels, and to exhibit them in public, if it is possible, though they are often the same, and to attempt to conceal the fact that they are the same, and to have splendid garments, and all other things for display, and to show that you are a man honored by the great, and to try to sup at their houses, or to be supposed to sup there, and as to your person to employ some mean arts, that you may appear to be more handsome and nobler than you are. These things you must contrive, if you choose to go by the second path in order not to be pitied.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied, Section 1

plain_english: The first approach is impossible and takes forever — trying to do what Zeus himself couldn't do: convince everyone what's good and what's bad. Do you have that power? No. You only have the power to convince yourself. And you haven't even done that yet. So why are you trying to persuade other people? Who has spent more time with you than you have with yourself? Who has more influence over you than you do? Who cares more about you than you do? So why haven't you convinced yourself to learn what you need to learn? Right now everything is backwards. Haven't you been working to learn how to be free from grief and anxiety? To not be crushed by life? To be truly free? Then you must have heard there's only one path to get there: give up the things that aren't up to you. Step back from them. Accept that they belong to other people. So when someone has an opinion about you — what kind of thing is that? It's not up to you. So it's nothing to you. It's nothing at all. But if you're still upset and disturbed by it, do you really think you understand what's good and what's bad?
original_excerpt: But the first way is both impracticable and long, to attempt the very thing which Zeus has not been able to do, to convince all men what things are good and bad. Is this power given to you? This only is given to you, to convince yourself; and you have not convinced yourself. Then I ask you, do you attempt to persuade other men? and who has lived so long with you as you with yourself? and who has so much power of convincing you as you have of convincing yourself; and who is better disposed and nearer to you than you are to yourself? How then have you not yet convinced yourself in order to learn? At present are not things upside down? Is this what you have been earnest about doing, to learn to be free from grief and free from disturbance, and not to be humbled (abject), and to be free? Have you not heard then that there is only one way which leads to this end, to give up (dismiss) the things which do not depend on the will, to withdraw from them, and to admit that they belong to others? For another man then to have an opinion about you, of what kind is it? It is a thing independent of the will—Then is it nothing to you? It is nothing. When then you are still vexed at this and disturbed, do you think that you are convinced about good and evil?
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied, Section 1
